strengths: Strong empirical results with state-of-the-art performance on both ScreenSpot-v2 (93.9%) and ScreenSpot-Pro (56.5%), particularly the +6.4% improvement on the more challenging benchmark
Well-motivated problem formulation: identifies genuine limitation of one-step GUI grounding methods (absence of visual feedback) and proposes intuitive interactive solution
Thorough experimental analysis including effective ablation studies, detailed training dynamics analysis with identified three-stage learning, and insightful cursor-in-box spatial reasoning test
Practical engineering contributions: cursor-centric focusing (CCF) strategy effective for high-resolution images, well-designed trajectory penalties preventing degenerate behaviors
Comprehensive baseline comparisons across both supervised fine-tuning and RL-based methods with detailed performance breakdown by UI categories
Adaptive movement strategy: model learns to use single steps for most examples but intelligently conducts more steps for difficult (small target) cases
Good presentation with clear writing, informative visualizations, and accessible methodology explanation with detailed implementation details
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily task reformulation + straightforward reward function design using standard GRPO, rather than methodological innovation; trajectory penalties are somewhat obvious solutions to prevent degenerate behaviors

Narrow evaluation scope: only two related benchmarks (ScreenSpot variants); no evaluation on other major GUI grounding datasets (Mind2Web, WebShop, MiniWoB++); no cross-domain or out-of-distribution tests

Generalization concerns: zero-shot performance collapses dramatically (88.8% → 36.3% with direct move), suggesting benefits are almost entirely from RL fine-tuning rather than learned robust spatial understanding; only tested with single base model

Contradiction between claims and evidence: paper claims multi-step movement is key contribution, but 95% of examples use single-step on ScreenSpot-v2 and only 9.4% use >1 step on ScreenSpot-Pro; benefits appear to come primarily from single-step improvement with visual feedback

CCF strategy has fundamental limitation: ~10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples have targets outside the focused area when initial prediction is poor; improvements on other baselines smaller (GTA1/GUI-G2: +3.9% each) when CCF applied separately

Hyperparameter choices lack justification: trajectory penalty weight wp=0.2 with higher false stop penalty 0.5 appears ad-hoc; no sensitivity analysis; cursor size (20×31) arbitrary with no ablations; format reward weight 0.1 unjustified

Training efficiency not thoroughly evaluated: requires 8 A100 GPUs but total training time not specified; computational cost comparison with baselines absent; impact of sampling multiple trajectories per example not quantified

Incomplete analysis of spatial reasoning: cursor-in-box improvement modest and causality unclear; claim that visual feedback improves general spatial understanding undermined by model's poor zero-shot performance; improvements may reflect task-specific overfitting rather than robust reasoning
Limited failure analysis: few negative examples in appendix; concerning behaviors (hallucinating action sequences, repeated predictions) not systematically analyzed or categorized

Training-inference mismatch and reproducibility concerns: resolution mismatch (1920×1080 training vs 4096×2160 testing); max steps mismatch (4 training vs flexible inference); online filtering and preprocessing may prevent exact reproduction; code release not mentioned

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation addressing spatial semantic alignment in GUI grounding through interactive visual feedback
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four GUI grounding benchmarks, online agentic tasks, and spatial reasoning datasets with extensive ablations
Strong data efficiency results: achieves 58.1% on ScreenSpot-Pro with only 8K training samples vs. 64K for GTA1, demonstrating sample efficiency
Thoughtful system design with trajectory penalties that prevent degenerate behaviors and clear demonstration of their necessity through ablations
Insightful analysis showing adaptive multi-step behavior on difficult cases and clever cursor-in-box test isolating spatial reasoning capability
Comprehensive implementation details and reproducibility information provided in extensive appendices
weaknesses: Inconsistent improvements across benchmarks: strong on ScreenSpot-Pro (+8.0%) but actually worse on OSWorld-G (-2.1% vs GTA1), raising concerns about generalization
Fair comparison issues: GUI-CURSOR trained at 1920×1080 while GTA1 at 4096×2160; applying GTA1 with cursor-centric focusing (CCF) narrows gap to 2.5%, suggesting resolution/CCF may drive improvements
Cursor-centric focusing (CCF) contribution is largely orthogonal to interactive cursor approach; CCF also benefits competing methods significantly (GTA1: +3.9%), complicating credit attribution

Significant unresolved limitation: ~10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples have targets cropped out of focused region, and model's ability to detect this failure mode is weak (31% detection, 20% false positive rate)
Limited conceptual novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (GRPO, standard rewards, trajectory penalties) for task reformulation rather than introducing fundamentally new methods
Incomplete failure analysis: no systematic breakdown of which target types/sizes/locations remain challenging; limited investigation of failure modes beyond isolated examples
Modest out-of-distribution generalization: spatial reasoning benchmark improvements are small (+1.9% to +5.3%), not strongly supporting claims of robust spatial reasoning
Computational cost concerns not adequately addressed: requires 8 A100 GPUs; training per-step time increases 2.4× (289→680 seconds); inference latency +0.3s on complex examples
